Thanks for proposing support for JWT authentication in the WebSocketClient [user]

The design and implementation raise a number of security-relevant implementation questions. I highlighted some library choices that need to be revisited, but the main question relates to use case and design of the properties. The OAuth 2 Token Provider service supports a standard method for obtaining Access Tokens from an Identity Provider. The proposed changes with a static file-based JWT do not provide a scalable or standards-oriented approach.

There is definitely value in supporting token-based authentication, but this needs to be implemented in a way that follows published standards for JWT generation.

As this will require some significant rework, it would be much better to provide more substantive details in the associated Jira issue. I would be glad to work through some of the design considerations there, and then return to considering a new pull request after considering the approach.

The proposed description mentions locating connections with load balancing, but that should not be the primary purpose of analysis rules.

On initial review, the rule itself seems too broad. Connection Load Balancing makes sense at very particular parts of a flow, and does not make sense in others. One anti-pattern is load balancing at every Processor, as opposed to just an initial source. Having a general rule that checks for the presence of load balancing one way or the other doesn't provide enough granularity to determine whether the implementation is good or bad.

Are there other use cases where this generalized approach fits?

Thanks for flagging this issue [user], however, there are several implementation concerns that need to be considered.

As background, the [INT96](https://parquet.apache.org/docs/file-format/implementationstatus/#physical-types) type is deprecated, although Parquet notes it is still commonly used. I question the value of introducing this support for a deprecated feature in the current ParquetReader. 

The Jira issue mentions Spark as the source, but is there a particular Spark version that still uses INT96? That would help determine whether this should be supported.

If it is something to consider supporting, it would be better to have an alternative ParquetReader implementation to avoid introducing this deprecated feature. In more depth on the implementation, the standard `ObjectLocalDateTimeFieldConverter` should not include any of this specialized conversion handling. I understand that it is referenced through the `AvroTypeUtil`, so decoupling and introducing an alternate implementation may be involved.

Given the way this processor is likely going to be used, I think we should be prescriptive here and avoid generating one flow file per listed file in the configured folder. Instead I would generate a single FlowFile with JSON content with an array of records, each record containing the metadata information of the listed files.

Assuming a folder with 50k files, that will avoid generating 50k flowfiles in one execution of the processor. By generating one single flowfile, a user could then use a first SliptRecord processor configured with 1000 records split, then a second SplitRecord with 1 record split, and finally a ForkRecord with path(s) for the fields that should be moved into flowfile attributes. This way the backpressure would do its job.

Thanks for proposing these changes [user] Honoring back pressure is an important improvement, but I think the interface naming and implementation needs to be reworked.

The `Pause` naming is very generic, and as this relates more specifically the consuming records, a more specific naming strategy would be more intuitive.

On the read side in the RecordProcessor classes, treating this as more of a conditional rather than `consumePause()` would be much clearer. There are some analogies to a [Semaphore](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/concurrent/Semaphore.html), although I don't think that actual class should be used here because of unnecessary complexity. The [ManagedBlocker](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/concurrent/ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker.html) seems a bit closer to what is intended here. What do you think about naming the basic interface something like `RecordProcessorBlocker`? That highlights the usage in `RecordProcessor` and also connotes blocking, which is the purpose of the abstraction. Perhaps `RecordProcessorLatch` could be better, inspired by the `CountDownLatch` class, but not necessarily tied to that implementation. The basic method could be `await()` following the `CountDownLatch` pattern.

I avoided adding an enumeration of header names and content types in earlier versions due to potential unclear boundaries on what to include, so I think this warrants some consideration.

For Header Names, I think we should be careful on the boundaries of what to include. Various RFC documents define standard headers, and other headers have become de facto standards. One other potential issue is that HTTP/2 lowercases header names. Most HTTP clients handle this translation for requests internally, but handling responses becomes more challenging. That reason alone makes me think that defining header names could be problematic when it comes to expecting particular HTTP protocol versions of client behavior.

On the Content Type side, there are also RFC standards, to which definitions should be tied.

In general, I recommend alphabetizing the enumeration values, and adding a reference comment such as:

```
/** RFC 4627 */
APPLICATION_JSON("application/json");
```

Even with that approach however, I think it is necessary to have a narrow set of types, and I would call it `MediaType` to align with the [IANA Registry of Media Types](https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/media-types.xhtml).

Although I know other clients like Spring Web include these enumerations, I consider the `nifi-web-client-api` more analogous to the JDK HttpClient and OkHttp, neither of which have these enumerations.

It may be worth considering a separate module, such as `nifi-web-client-shared`, which includes these enumerations, but does not carry the same implications of the API, which is part of the `nifi-web-client-provider-api` Controller Service definition.

Those are some initial thoughts, and I would be interested in your responses.

Thanks for proposing this integration with Camel [user], however, I'm going to vote this down based the general impedance mismatch between Camel and NiFi.

In past years, NiFi has had other Processors that supported generalized framework integration, including Apache Flume and Spring Framework. Although this type of generalized component seems appealing at first, it presents a large number of integration and troubleshooting challenges. Generalized framework integration often requires a large number of dependencies, only some of which are actually required at runtime. Due to the abstract nature of such integrations, using them requires a thorough understanding of both NiFi and the integrated framework. This leads to troubleshooting difficulties when attempting to track down behavior or performance issues, making it unclear whether the problem is with NiFi or with the integrated framework.

This is not a negative reflection on Apache Camel or other generalized framework. It reflects a number of lessons learned from historical attempts to integrate disparate frameworks in NiFi 1, which were abandoned and removed in NiFi 2.

This is also not ruling out the potential value of such integrations for certain use cases. For this reason, I recommend providing the components in a separate GitHub repository as a way to gather feedback and improvements.

I also tested the processors and found the following missing features:

**SSL**
The processors cannot work with an SSL enabled server. SSL support is a basic feature in NiFi processors so I think we should add it in this PR or in a follow-up Jira.

**Optimistic locking**
Couchbase supports optimistic locking via `CAS` (Compare-And-Swap id of a document version) and `replace()` method. Both Get and Put processors retrieve the CAS of the document and add it as a FlowFile attribute but it is not used later. The Put processor updates the document using `upsert()` (unconditional update). The processor could be improved to optionally use `replace()` and CAS with optimistic locking (fails if CAS does not match). Thanks for highlighting this issue with handling default values [user]

There are a few implementation issues to consider, but before evaluating those details, I think the implementation needs to be considered from a different angle.

As noted in the Jira issue, the fundamental problem is that placeholder values like `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` do not align with the expectation of the Record Schema that the default value is a specific value, such as a timestamp. I agree that attempting to handle such placeholders introduces a level of complexity that does not fit well with the current overall Record Schema design. However, I'm not sure that ignoring all default values in a table is the best option.

At minimum, the default behavior should be preserved, which attempts to read use the default value if defined.

One option to consider is attempting to parse the returned default value according to the data type defined. In cases like `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, the parsing would fail, and in that case, the default value could be ignored. This should be logged at an informational level. Taking this approach avoids introducing a new property, and allows the component to support as many default values as possible.

The `ErrorHandlingStrategy` enum could be renamed to `ExceptionCategory`, and then the Processor could implement the appropriate logic. The difference is that the Service API and implementation define the category of the exception, but the Processor is responsible for deciding how to handle it. The net result is similar, but it keeps the responsibility more clearly defined.

2. For this initial pull request, I recommend removing the Couchbase NARs from the `nifi-assembly`. Although the Service API and Processor NARs have no other dependencies, which is great, the Standard Service NAR includes the Couchbase Core IO, which is about 30 MB. The reason it is so large is that it includes shaded versions of multiple libraries, including gRPC, Jackson, and Netty. Specifically, it includes platform-dependent native libraries from Netty. From a dependency management perspective, this makes it impossible to override the shaded version of Netty, creating potential vulnerability issues when Netty publishes vulnerabilities. Couchbase is not unique in this way, but it is less common. Given the size and shading, I think it is best to leave it out of the standard binary distribution, at least for the initial version.

Thanks for the PR [user] and for taking the feedback from the previous PR into consideration.

The approach of navigating to just `/process-groups/{parentId}` (without the component in the URL) and using a store flag to trigger selection afterward avoids the regression that affected the previous PR -- search-based centering is preserved. That's a good improvement.

One concern I have is the same issue I flagged in the [previous PR](https://github.com/apache/nifi/pull/9849#pullrequestreview-2297247069): the subscription chains in `canvas.component.ts` fire twice during cross-PG navigation -- once when the route changes (against stale store data) and again when the store finishes loading. I've confirmed this with runtime instrumentation: during a leave-PG operation, the viewport-restore subscriber fires first while `selectCurrentProcessGroupId` still holds the child PG ID (stale), and then fires again after the parent PG loads with the correct ID. This isn't something introduced by this PR -- it's a latent issue in the existing code. But this PR's `leavingProcessGroupId` guard implicitly relies on that double-fire to work correctly: the first stale firing is filtered out because `currentProcessGroupId` still equals `leavingProcessGroupId`, and only the second firing passes the guard. This means `restoreViewport()` is also dispatched twice per leave -- once against stale state and once against the correct state. Building on top of that double-fire makes it harder to address later.

I think it would be worth addressing the double-fire directly as part of this change. All three subscription chains in `canvas.component.ts` (viewport restore, single-component selection, and bulk selection) share the same pattern:

```typescript
switchMap(() => this.store.select(selectCurrentProcessGroupId)),
distinctUntilChanged(),
switchMap(() => this.store.select(/* chain-specific selector */)),
```

A sync guard can be inserted after `distinctUntilChanged()` to ensure the store and route agree before proceeding:

```typescript
switchMap(() => this.store.select(selectCurrentProcessGroupId)),
distinctUntilChanged(),
concatLatestFrom(() => this.store.select(selectProcessGroupIdFromRoute)),
filter(([storeId, routeId]) => storeId === routeId),
switchMap(() => this.store.select(/* chain-specific selector */)),
```

Both selectors already exist. This prevents any of the three chains from acting on stale data during cross-PG navigation and eliminates the redundant `restoreViewport()` dispatch.

With that in place, the child PG selection could be handled entirely in the `leaveProcessGroup$` effect as a two-step navigation: first navigate to the parent PG (letting the viewport restore as usual), then listen for `loadProcessGroupComplete` and dispatch `navigateWithoutTransform` to select the child PG. This would avoid needing the new store state (`leavingProcessGroupId`, the action, the reducer case, and the selector) since the effect can capture the current PG ID at the time `leaveProcessGroup` is dispatched and use it after the load completes.

Happy to discuss further or help work through the details.

Not sure why specifically with this PR but it feels like we have a timing issue and I guess the transitive upgrade is just exposing a long standing race condition issue is those tests.

In `nifi-docker/dockermaven/integration-test.sh`, we do:

```sh
if docker exec "${container_name}" bash -c " echo Running < /dev/tcp/${ip}/${port}"; then
```

Jetty binds early but we don't have everything ready yet. So I think this logic should be improved with something along the lines of

```sh
echo "Waiting for NiFi REST API (expect status: 400)"
max_iterations=10
sleep_time=10
sleep ${sleep_time}
for i in $(seq 1 "${max_iterations}"); do
    echo "Waiting for NiFi REST API - iteration: ${i}"
    status="$(docker exec "${container_name}" bash -c \
        "curl -ksSo /dev/null -w %{http_code} -m 10 --retry 5 --retry-all-errors --retry-max-time 60 https://${ip}:${port}/nifi-api/authentication/configuration" || true)"
    if [ "${status}" = "400" ]; then
        echo "NiFi REST API responded with ${status}"
        break
    fi
    if [ "${i}" -eq "${max_iterations}" ]; then
        echo "NiFi REST API did not return 400 within expected time (last status: ${status})"
        exit 1
    fi
    sleep ${sleep_time}
done
```

A few non-blocking suggestions:

**1. Missing `[user]` on the new getter.** `getClusterNodeProtocolHttpVersion()` has a full Javadoc block but no `[user]` tag. It won't fail checkstyle (`allowMissingReturnTag=true`), but it's inconsistent with the coding standard now that the method is documented:

```java
/**
 * ...
 * [user] the configured cluster node protocol HTTP version, or the default when the property is missing or blank
 */
public String getClusterNodeProtocolHttpVersion() {
```

**2. Property scope is broader than the name suggests.** The `webClientService()` bean this configures isn't only used for request replication — it's also injected into `NarRestApiClient`, `AssetsRestApiClient`, `NiFiRestApiClient`, and `StandardUploadRequestReplicator`. So `nifi.cluster.node.protocol.http.version` effectively governs the HTTP version for all framework intra-cluster HTTP clients. They're all node-to-node operations so the name is defensible, but it would be worth noting in the admin-guide entry that it applies to all framework cluster HTTP communication, not just request replication.

**3. Consider being case-insensitive.** `HttpClient.Version.valueOf(configured)` requires an exact match, so `http_2` / `http_1_1` would silently fall back to the default with a warning. Upper-casing the trimmed value first would avoid that surprise:

```java
return HttpClient.Version.valueOf(configured.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
```

**4. Track the stopgap.** The Jira notes this isn't intended as a permanent solution to run system tests on HTTP/1.1, but nothing in the code points back to that intent. Could we add a short comment next to the `nifi.cluster.node.protocol.http.version=HTTP_1_1` lines in the system-test configs (or reference a follow-up Jira for the upstream Jetty 12.1.10 `RST_STREAM` regression) so the override isn't forgotten once Jetty is fixed?

The design is sound and the classification logic is careful. I verified the three behaviors the feature depends on: destinations do stay running during the drain (only the producer-barrier set is ever passed to `scheduleComponents(..., STOPPED)`), producers stay stopped afterwards so the later empty-queue check remains meaningful, and unsupported topologies are rejected before anything is stopped. The cluster wait correctly refuses to treat a connection as drained when a node fails to report queue status.

My concerns are concentrated in the failure and cancellation paths of `RemovedConnectionDrainCoordinator`, where components that the framework stopped on its own initiative can be left stopped with no restore and no log entry. Details inline; the first two are the ones I would want addressed before merge.

[claude-opus-4.8] Marking the review I just left as Request Changes. The detailed comments are in https://github.com/apache/nifi/pull/11570#pullrequestreview-5012405715; this is only to set the review state correctly, not to add new findings.

The two items I consider blocking are both in `RemovedConnectionDrainCoordinator`, and both leave components that the framework stopped on its own initiative in a stopped state with no restore and nothing in the log:

1. **Line 136** catches only `LifecycleManagementException`, but in a cluster the drain wait replicates a `POST` with `performVerification = true` and can throw `IllegalClusterStateException` or `ConnectingNodeMutableRequestException`, both unchecked. An ordinary cluster membership change during the 30-second drain is enough to trigger it, and the producers are never restarted.

2. **Line 127** returns success without checking `isCancelled()`. If cancellation lands on the poll that observes the queues empty, `FlowUpdateResource` goes on to stop the destinations too and then returns before reaching the block that would restart anything, so producers and destinations are both left stopped even though this class is documented to restore on cancellation.

The remaining comments (classifier reason naming, null group id treated as retained, the `appendFailureDetail` NPE, missing logging, the request-type literal, the stale workflow comment, and the disabled clustered test) are worth addressing but I would not hold the PR on them individually.

The overall approach is good and the classification logic is careful. I verified that destinations stay running during the drain, that producers stay stopped so the later empty-queue check remains meaningful, that unsupported topologies are rejected before anything is stopped, and that the cluster wait does not treat a non-reporting node as drained.

After a rebase onto current `main`, out-of-range bends on `entity.bends` would skip `sanitizePosition` and still reach d3. `component.bends` can remain as a nested DTO copy, but it is not what the connector canvas draws.

Suggested fix: sanitize `entity.bends` (and `component.bends` if that nested copy is still present) with the existing `${id}:bend:${index}` ids. Extend the new tests so a positionless connection with an out-of-range **entity** bend is clamped and warned, not only `component.bends`.
